extracted.intended_audience: reporters and journalists covering speeches and meetings for newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for reporting speeches and covering meetings for newspaper stories, including how to quote, paraphrase, structure meeting stories, verify facts, and avoid common mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct quotation — correctness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, direct quotation does not demand the literal reproduction of the speaker's words. They may be quoted directly if they convey: 1. The substance of the remark, in full accuracy. 2. The spirit in which the remark was made. 3. The typical language used by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotation is the safest method for handling controversial material; quoted material should be given 'quite as the speaker said it, with no improvements, embellishings, deletions, or softenings.' Literal word-for-word is ideal but not required if substance, spirit, and typical language are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect quotation (reported speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect quoting presents the speaker's ideas mainly but not entirely in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: (i) permits modest condensing; (2) allows the reporter to untangle intricate sentences and smooth out grammar; (3) covers portions the reporter failed to gather precisely enough for direct quotation. Keep in-context considerations strongly in mind so impact remains unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase — reporter's own words
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase is when the reporter uses his own words rather than the speaker's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows more thorough abbreviation, repairs broken diction, brings clarity to utterances that relied on gesture/facial expression/inflection, and translates those aids into coherent prose. The reporter must select words that have the same net effect on readers as the speaker's original words — rephrasing to obtain accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-context consideration for quotes and paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations and paraphrases must remain in focus and in context; snatches 'here and a snatch there' will not be accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider the surrounding context of the remark; changing context can change impact and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give him a break — remedying bad grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: The general practice is for the reporter to remedy the speaker's bad grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spoken sentence isn't twin to the sentence that is read; amend grammar within limits allowed by offering 'the substance and spirit of a speech, in typical language.' Do not quote verbatim if faithful reproduction makes the speaker seem ridiculous when the audience originally regarded him as earnest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotation for debatable/controversial matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotation is the safest method of handling controversial material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrases may seem inaccurate for debatable material; offering such statements in direct quotation is evidence of careful, faithful, objective reporting and places responsibility on the speaker rather than the newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the ham-sandwich lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Shun leads in which the speaker is topped and bottomed by a slice of quotation (a quotation 'sandwiched' around identification and detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ham-sandwich leads force the reader to re-inflect the sentence mentally; identification and news information must appear in the lead but should not be placed so as to break the flow of the quoted passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of speaker identification and lead composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The news identification of the speaker frequently is the chief reason the talk was worth a story; the reporter should put this identification into the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter need not follow the speaker's chronology; reorder material so the most important point gets prominence in the written version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit transitional/filler phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, omit transition or connecting sentences such as 'Then turning to...' and filler remarks like 'I think' and 'I believe' unless they are essential qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paragraphing to indicate new topics rather than reproducing the speaker's connective tissue; remove speaker pauses or breath-taking devices that add little to the printed story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose attributive verbs carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The language has many ways of expressing 'he said'; the reporter should know variants but watch their color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbs that imply validation or partisanship (e.g., 'he pointed out' suggests 'beyond contradiction'); distinguish objective words ('he contradicted') from partisan ones ('he refuted'). Prune phrasing that underwrites the validity of the speaker's argument, especially on controversial topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accrediting in paraphrase-heavy paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a speech is offered mainly in paraphrase, each paragraph should contain an accrediting so that readers will be reminded that the speaker rather than the newspaper made the statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'he said' in the top rather than the bottom sentence of the paragraph to emphasize that the newspaper is reflecting someone else's declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must present the five Ws and attract casual readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead plays a point to attract casual readers and presents the five Ws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead may be a quotation, a name, the gist of a resolution, or another item of potential general interest. It should hook casual readers first; then follow with a rapid summary for other readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize nonmember/casual readers first
rubrics_metrics.description: In devising a story for diverse readers, the practice is to satisfy the nonmembers (casual readers) first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a strong lead and rapid summary (enough for casual readers); then expand for members and devoted readers with detailed accounts of principal speeches and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting story block structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended block layout for full meeting stories: Block 1: Lead; Block 2: Summary paragraph of speeches or business; Block 3: Summary paragraph of the other; Block 4: Catch-all; Block 5: Expansion of lead matter; Block 6: Expansion of block 2; Block 7: Expansion of block 3; Block 8: Texts of resolutions mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks 2 and 3 are interchangeable; structure keeps meeting stories clear and prevents overly parallel presentation. A full story built on this plan will be at least 500 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter meeting-story forms and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: If space is limited, a shorter meeting story should concentrate on a few peaks; two forms are suggested: First form (preferred): Lead, summary of the rest, details of lead. Second form: Lead, elaboration of lead, summary of rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first form is preferable because it better highlights the whole meeting at the top of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin speaker paragraphs with the speaker's name
rubrics_metrics.description: In longer stories, speeches presented in expanded blocks should begin with the speaker's name, e.g., 'Mr. Finch said in part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting a paragraph with the speaker's name prevents a rapid reader from missing the start of a new address and confusing it with the previous quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify program and last-minute changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The first information the reporter needs is about last-minute changes in the program: which speakers are coming, timing of business meetings, availability of advance copies of addresses, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the press-relations official or the man in immediate charge of the program; find out what the official expects to be the backbone of the meeting and what parts look like the best copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press-relations official but maintain editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large meetings often have a press chairman whose duty is to help the reporter give the meeting 'a good press.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official's assistance for facts, names, and advance copies, but do not let him dictate how the story is written. Be alert that publicity people may try to slant the story to reflect the organization's viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take notes per speech/phase on separate sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the notes for each speech or each phase of the business meeting upon a separate piece of paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheets can be shuffled to bring the best material to the top of the pile, making it easier to assemble the story's sequence and pick the strongest material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy test — willingness to show notes to speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter has a final and simple test for the accuracy of material: if he's perfectly willing to go to the speaker and tell what material he expects to use and how the quotations will read, he has no fear of a distorted or inaccurate story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reporter would rather not confront the speaker, something is wrong with those notes (incomplete or incorrect). Use this willingness as a conscience-based accuracy check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation (running story / writing from memory) should be cautious
rubrics_metrics.description: As the reporter becomes more expert, he may experiment: (a) try a running story (write the story as the speaker talks) or (b) sit on notes and attempt to write from memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These experiments hinge on judging whether a remark is worth recording and require photographic memory or notes on hand; they are for experienced reporters only and should be attempted cautiously with notes available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 1: Misunderstanding significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to understand the significance of various actions or speeches (e.g., dismissing an officer's election that actually breaks a long precedent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate context and background to determine whether routine-seeming items have deeper news value; do not be lazy by assuming ordinariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 2: Overplaying minor incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Overplaying flashy minor incidents at the expense of more important happenings (e.g., leading with a comic or freak angle while ignoring major resolutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose leads and emphasis based on significance, not just color or amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 3: Writing a dry, boring story
rubrics_metrics.description: A dry, boring story often results from failing to dig into the meeting's background and finding the available stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every meeting of substantial attendance usually contains multiple good stories; reporters should probe background and translate specialist jargon for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 4: Writing biased or partisan copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing personal favor (e.g., good meals) or editorial positions to color news coverage, resulting in bias or partisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain objectivity on the news page; do not reward hospitality with favorable coverage or let editorial dislike lead to negative slant in news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 5: Writing for insiders ('club members') instead of general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing copy that appeals mainly to insiders and assumes knowledge rather than making the story accessible to general readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General readers come first; the top paragraphs must have broad appeal or the piece will be ignored by the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six chances to ruin a meeting story — 6: Producing structurally imperfect (muddy) stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a story that must be read in its entirety before the main currents of action and speech are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid chronological muddiness; plan structure so the main points are clear early, using the recommended block organization and careful paragraphing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand types of readers and tailor content
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers divided into: (i) casual readers, (ii) 'club members', and (iii) nonmembers with latent curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfy casual readers with the lead and summary; then offer elaborations for devoted readers and club members. Beware of leading with an angle that makes the organization appear as a freak and alienates members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use volunteer helpers and secretaries carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect volunteer helpers eager to enlighten the reporter but typically partisan; secretaries often provide good official abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use helpers for guidance, but gauge their bias; when meetings subdivide, attend the best gathering and conscript helpers to cover others; secretaries' official abstracts are reliable sources for summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run human-interest/features as separate 'with' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Features or human-interest material often can adorn the reporter's work but should preferably be run as separate stories rather than forced into the straight-news version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A collection of 'convention sidelights' makes a readable 'with' story; save personal touches and tidbits for separate treatment to keep the main meeting story focused.
